## Overview

The Makaa, also called Maka, are a Bantu ethnic group living in the southern rain forest zone of Cameroon, primarily in the northern portions of the Upper Nyong division of the East Province. Major settlements include Abong-Mbang, Doumé, and Nguélémendouka, while some villages extend into the Centre Province. The Makaa language has an estimated 89,500 speakers; the related Byep language had an estimated 9,500 speakers in 1988. Makaa territory includes the northern part of Haut-Nyong department and areas around the Nyong River. Makaa folk culture, as described in the sources, is expressed especially through subsistence farming, hunting, house construction, clan organisation, oral traditions, and continuing practices associated with Christianity, traditional medicine, and animism.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The traditional Makaa house is a rectangular structure made from mud bricks held together by a bamboo frame. Its A-shaped roof is covered with raffia palm leaves, although tin and aluminium roofing have become more common. Wealthier Makaa and residents of larger villages and towns also live in modern concrete-block houses. Makaa settlements typically follow existing roads, producing linear villages in which houses face the road and are backed by forest.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They do identify axes and machetes as tools used to clear fields, traps as the primary hunting tool, and firearms as increasingly used for hunting.

## Music & performance

 They describe oral traditions concerning the migration of Makaa-Njem-speaking peoples and their encounters with Baka nomads. According to these traditions, migrants moving deeper into the rain forest enlisted the Baka as guides through force or diplomacy. These accounts include the founding of settlements such as Bung-Ngwang, described as meaning “bathing area in the Nyong River,” and Mess'a Mena, described as meaning “crossroads.” These settlements were later renamed Abong-Mbang and Messaména.

## Festivals & rituals

 They state that the vast majority of Makaa practice at least nominal Christianity, divided fairly evenly between Catholicism and Protestantism. Vestiges of native animism persist, especially in traditional medicine, and folk superstitions including belief in witchcraft also remain.

## Foodways

Makaa subsistence farming is based on small fields cut into forest clearings with axes and machetes and then burned. Major crops are manioc, plantains, and maize; bananas, cocoyams, groundnuts, and various fruits are grown in smaller quantities. Livestock generally include goats, sheep, pigs, and chickens, which may be left to roam unattended. Hunting is especially common in smaller villages, and bushmeat caught with traps or firearms has become an important, though unsustainable, source of income for many people. A smaller number of Makaa have obtained financial success in cocoa and coffee plantations.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources document Makaa oral traditions concerning migration and settlement. Makaa-Njem-speaking peoples are described as having entered present-day Cameroon from the Congo River basin or modern Chad between the 14th and 17th centuries. Their oral traditions recount encounters with Baka nomads in the rain forest and describe the establishment and renaming of settlements, including Bung-Ngwang and Mess'a Mena.

## Language & religion

Makaa, also called Maka or South Makaa, is a Bantu language of Cameroon and is not intelligible with North Makaa. The language varieties described include Bésáp, Bébánde, Mbwas, Byáp, and Békol; Byáp and Asón are distinguished from Northern Maka. Related dialect names in the Makaa people article include Bebent, Mbwaanz, Sekunda, Byep, and Besep. The Makaa language uses cedillas to indicate nasal vowels and diacritics for tones. Makaa practice Christianity, with Catholicism and Protestantism both widespread. Native animism continues especially in traditional medicine, while belief in witchcraft remains among folk superstitions.
